claims.text: The as-cast Al0.3CoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% Zr enhances bonding at dual-phase lamellar boundaries.
Zr additions introduce beneficial lattice distortions at or near lamellar interfaces.
Enhanced interfacial bonding and lattice distortion reduce stress concentrations at internal boundaries.
Reduced boundary stress concentrations suppress microcrack nucleation.
Suppressing microcrack nucleation produces simultaneous improvements in tensile strength and room-temperature ductility.
Annealing near 850 °C for 30–60 minutes uniformly distributes Zr.
The proposed short anneal near 850 °C avoids formation of brittle Zr-rich intermetallic phases.
Zr atoms have a larger atomic radius than the relevant constituent atoms and therefore create local lattice distortions.
Zr-induced local lattice distortions improve the coherency and bonding of dual-phase lamellar interfaces.
Improved lamellar-interface bonding promotes more uniform plastic deformation during tensile loading.
The Zr modification may promote deformation-twin formation during tensile loading.
Zr in solid solution increases tensile yield strength through solid-solution strengthening.
Reduced microcrack nucleation and enhanced interfacial toughness increase tensile ductility.
The Zr-modified alloy retains the dual-phase lamellar architecture.
The unmodified as-cast eutectic alloy has high strength but limited ductility because microcracks initiate at weakly bonded internal boundaries.
The beneficial effect requires Zr to remain in solid solution or modify interfaces without forming brittle Zr-rich intermetallics.
Excessive Zr segregation or Zr-rich precipitation can reduce both ductility and strength.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is the conventional as-cast alloy, whereas the experiment applies identical homogenization conditions to the 0% Zr control. This makes the experimental control an annealed alloy rather than the stated as-cast baseline.

The boundary field excludes specimens containing brittle Zr-rich intermetallics from the claimed beneficial regime, but the falsification rule treats formation of those phases as direct falsification rather than as failure to satisfy the hypothesis's stated boundary conditions.
